passage: I'm Rajni, and I work at a ration-card help desk. One afternoon Vishal came in furious because his form had been rejected for the second time. He slammed his hand on the counter and shouted that we were useless. My heart raced and my first urge was to shout back. Instead I lowered my voice, took a half step back and said, "I can see this has been really frustrating. Let me look at the reason together with you." He was still loud, but he stopped hitting the counter. I said I couldn't change the rule, but I could tell him exactly what was missing so he could fix it that day. I also kept my hand near the bell for the security guard. If he hadn't calmed down, I would have walked away and called the guard.

qa.a: His form had been rejected for the second time.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as Vishal shouted, and how was it handled?
qa.a: Rajni felt alarmed and angry, with a racing heart and an urge to shout back, but Rajni spoke more quietly and stepped back.

qa.q: Why did Rajni keep a hand near the bell?
qa.a: Safety comes first, so Rajni was ready to get the guard if calm did not work.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when Rajni offered to look at the reason with him?
qa.a: Possibly heard, and a little less angry, since he stopped hitting the counter, though he was still loud.

grounding: A young adult facing a furious person speaks more quietly, keeps distance, offers a calm way out and keeps safety in mind.

passage: Note from Irawati, clinic supervisor. At 4 pm a visitor stood at the desk and shouted at Asif about the wait, moving closer and jabbing a finger. Asif kept his hands visible and his voice low. He said, "You've waited a long time and I'm sorry it's been so hard. I can't change the queue, but I can check where your name is and tell you how long it's likely to be." The visitor kept shouting for a while. Asif stepped back and offered a chair away from the counter and a glass of water. When the shouting turned to threats, he said calmly, "I want to help, but I can't do it while I'm being threatened," and signalled me. I came over, and the visitor left after a minute. I thanked Asif and suggested a break; his hands were shaking.

qa.q: What did Asif offer the visitor besides a chair?
What might Asif have been feeling while his hands shook?
qa.a: Probably shaken or scared after the threats, though he stayed calm outwardly.

qa.q: Why was signalling Irawati the right move?
qa.a: When calm did not work and threats began, safety meant getting help.

qa.q: How might the visitor have felt in the waiting area?
qa.a: Frustrated and helpless about the wait, which may explain the shouting though it does not excuse threats.

grounding: A young adult facing a furious visitor lowers his voice, keeps distance, offers a calm way out and gets help when threats begin, seen by a supervisor.
